title: Problems associated with clinical evaluation of antianginal medications.
abstract: Assessing the efficacy of antianginal medications is not as easy as it might first appear. Many factors, including the protocol, the subjects chosen for study and the physicians conducting the trial, may produce study bias and thereby yield equivocal results. Objectively attempting to quantitate a subjective event such as angina inherently poses many difficulties. The variable nature of anginal episodes makes identification of attacks, or conversely, elimination of such attacks, difficult to assess. In terms of the protocol, it is necessary to determine what indexes will be used as criteria of efficacy, what doses, either standard or maximally tolerated, will be used for study and what measures will be taken to nullify placebo effect. In terms of patient selection, the varying methods of confirming the diagnosis of ischemia and the questions of concurrent illness, compliance and life-style alterations are all factors that can make findings difficult to elucidate. Finally, investigator bias may be introduced into study results because of prestudy prejudice, involvement in data acquisition and interpretation of findings. It is unlikely that any investigator or group of investigators will ever produce a protocol applicable to all types of antianginal medications that will be universally convincing. Conclusions regarding the efficacy of any antianginal medication will undoubtedly continue to be predicated on assessments made by independent investigators using a variety of research protocols, none of which is likely to be perfect.

screening.rationale: Narrative article focused on trial methodology and strategies to 'nullify placebo effect', meeting inclusion for placebo science about trial methodology.

classification.summary: Discusses challenges in clinical trials of antianginal drugs, including measurement of angina, protocol choices, and methods to address or nullify placebo effects and investigator bias.

title: Depot-glucagon in the treatment of McArdle's disease.
journal: Australian and New Zealand journal of medicine
abstract: Glucagon has been reported to improve exercise tolerance in some patients with myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle's disease) but a placebo effect was not excluded in previous trials. A single-blind controlled trial of glucagon in a patient with myophosphorylase deficiency is described. Although an improved exercise endurance of the forearm muscles was demonstrated with both short-acting and depot-glucagon, this was not statistically significant when compared with placebo or no treatment.

screening.rationale: Single-blind controlled trial in a patient that compared glucagon, placebo, and no treatment and reported placebo/no-treatment comparisons, so placebo-related causal contrasts were examined.

classification.summary: Reported a single-blind controlled trial in one patient with McArdle's disease and found improved forearm exercise endurance with glucagon that was not statistically significant compared with placebo or no treatment.
classification.key_finding: Improved endurance with short-acting and depot glucagon did not differ significantly from placebo or no treatment (N=1).

title: Incidence of side effects during the application of placebo and active therapy (Tobanum) in patients suffering from hypertension, angina pectoris and arrhythmia.
journal: International journal of clinical pharmacology, therapy, and toxicology
journal_abbrev: Int J Clin Pharmacol Ther Toxicol
abstract: In a single blind clinical trial the effects of Tobanum (chloranolol), a beta-adrenergic receptor blocker, on 450 patients were examined. The side effects were detected by placebo control. Complaints were recorded on a questionnaire in the placebo period as well as in the active treatment period. Every fourth patient reported complaints in the placebo period and every third had a new complaint in the active period. Qualitative and quantitative analysis of the complaints indicated that Tobanum has mainly cardiorespiratory side effects judging from the beta-blocker characteristics. The study draws attention to the need for awareness of complaints in the placebo period for correct evaluation of side effects.

screening.rationale: Clinical trial explicitly measured and reported adverse events (complaints) occurring during the placebo period, addressing placebo/nocebo responses.

classification.summary: Reported that 25% of patients recorded complaints during the placebo period and about 33% had new complaints during active Tobanum treatment, highlighting placebo-period side effects.
classification.key_finding: Found ~25% reported complaints during placebo and ~33% had new complaints during active beta-blocker treatment.

title: Alcohol and aggression: pharmacological versus expectancy effects.

screening.rationale: Title indicates an empirical balanced-placebo study contrasting pharmacological and expectancy effects of alcohol on aggression, so placebo/expectancy is the object of study.

classification.summary: Compared pharmacological versus expectancy (told-drink) effects of alcohol on aggression using a balanced/placebo design in human adults.

title: The placebo effect: a controversy.
journal: Journal of the Royal Society of Health

screening.rationale: Title and journal indicate a substantive commentary on the placebo effect (controversy/interpretation), meeting inclusion for placebo science commentary despite missing abstract.

classification.summary: Discusses debate and controversy surrounding the placebo effect, its interpretation, and implications for clinical practice and physician–patient relations.

title: Offspring of alcoholics have enhanced antagonistic placebo response.
abstract: In this study, 85 college-age men who reported normal drinking practices believed they were drinking malt liquor when they actually drank dealcoholized beer. Following drinking, 11 subjects with an alcoholic biological father showed a significantly larger heart rate decrease (p less than .05) than subjects with a nonalcoholic father. The results are discussed in terms of opponent process and classical conditioning theories of addiction, and the etiological pathway from risk factor to final manifestation of alcoholism.

screening.rationale: Experimental deception study examined physiological placebo (de-alcoholized beer believed to be alcoholic) and compared placebo responses by family-history, so placebo response was an object of study.

classification.summary: Tested college men given de-alcoholized beer believed to be alcoholic and found offspring of alcoholic fathers showed larger heart-rate decreases, consistent with conditioned/opponent-process accounts.
classification.key_finding: Offspring of alcoholic fathers had a significantly larger heart-rate decrease after drinking de-alcoholized beer believed to be alcoholic (p < .05).

title: Placebo-like effects of education about behavior therapy.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available and the title suggests placebo-like effects of education but methods and whether placebo/nocebo was a primary object of study are unclear.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated the study examined placebo-like effects of education about behavior therapy but methods and findings were not reported in the record.

title: Behavioral and emotional factors and treatment responses in a study of anovulatory infertile women.
abstract: In a controlled treatment study of 49 anovulatory infertile women, responses to clomiphene citrate (CC) and placebo treatments were compared and associations of behavioral and emotional factors with treatment responses were investigated. In the first treatment series, ovulation occurred in 20 of 24 women in the CC group and 8 of 22 women in the placebo group. Pregnancy was achieved by 11 women during CC treatment and 3 women during placebo treatment. Overall, 28 women completed the protocol and 21 withdrew. Those who achieved pregnancy (n = 14) did not differ significantly from the ovulation-only group (n = 22) on pretreatment measures of emotional, behavioral, and personality factors including the Hopkins Symptom Checklist (HSCL-90), Eysenck Personality Inventory, Langner Screening Scale, Mood Analog Scale, Social Adjustment Scale, Mooney Problem Checklist, and the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI). Conclusions were that a placebo response was observed in both ovulation and pregnancy, but psychologic factors as measured in this sample were not associated with these treatment outcomes.

screening.rationale: Controlled clinical trial compared clomiphene vs placebo and analyzed placebo-arm responses and psychological predictors, so placebo response was an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared clomiphene versus placebo in 49 anovulatory infertile women, observed ovulation and pregnancies in the placebo arm, and found baseline psychological measures did not predict treatment outcomes.
classification.key_finding: Placebo arm showed ovulation (8/22) and pregnancies (3), and pretreatment emotional/ personality scales were not associated with ovulation or pregnancy outcomes.

title: Clonidine benefits children with attention deficit disorder and hyperactivity: report of a double-blind placebo-crossover therapeutic trial.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry

screening.rationale: No abstract available and title indicates an efficacy double-blind placebo-crossover trial of clonidine in children with ADHD, but no evidence the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm responses.

classification.summary: No abstract available; appeared to be a 1985 double-blind placebo-crossover trial testing clonidine versus placebo in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

title: Lack of efficacy of polysorbate 60 in the treatment of male pattern baldness.
abstract: Anecdotal reports have indicated that the nonionic detergent polysorbate 60 may be of some value in male pattern baldness. In this double-blind placebo-controlled trial, a photographic and objective scalp measurement system was developed to assess new hair growth. No significant difference was detected between subjects treated for 16 weeks with polysorbate 60 and control subjects treated with glycerin, indicating that polysorbate 60 is ineffective. Of the 141 subjects who completed the trial, 25% perceived that they grew new hair, 67% said they did not, and 8% were uncertain. Subject-reported new hair growth did not correlate with measurements, indicating that the placebo effect may be a major factor in reports of baldness "cures".

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial that reported and analyzed participant-reported new hair growth (placebo response) and its mismatch with objective measures.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial found no objective benefit of polysorbate 60 versus glycerin for male pattern baldness and reported that 25% of participants perceived new hair growth, suggesting a placebo response contributed to anecdotal reports.
classification.key_finding: No significant objective hair growth difference between polysorbate 60 and glycerin (N=141); 25% reported perceived improvement despite no measurement correlation.

title: The effect of subcutaneous nerve stimulation (SCNS) on pain associated with osteoarthritis of the hip.
abstract: A novel form of subcutaneous nerve stimulation (SCNS) was recently introduced for the relief of chronic pain. We present a study using this form of SCNS applied over the radial, median and saphenous nerves in patients with clinically diagnosed osteoarthritis of the hip. Acceptable pain relief was obtained in 60% of patients receiving stimulation, however, comparable analgesia was achieved in a control group, who received no electrical stimulation through similarly placed needles. We suggest that these results may be explained by the ability of SCNS to evoke a placebo response. The efficacy of the placebo effect and the ethical implications of its use in clinical practice are discussed.

screening.rationale: Empirical clinical study that reported comparable analgesia in a no-stimulation control and discussed this as a placebo response, making placebo the object of analysis and discussion.

classification.summary: Reported that 60% of patients receiving subcutaneous nerve stimulation had acceptable pain relief, but a control group with needles but no stimulation experienced comparable analgesia, which authors attributed to a placebo response and discussed ethical implications.
classification.key_finding: Found comparable analgesia in stimulated and no-stimulation control groups (60% responders in stimulation arm), suggesting a strong placebo analgesia.

title: Comparative acceptance of three transdermal nitroglycerin placebo patches.
abstract: Factors that might affect patient acceptance of transdermal drug-delivery system patches were evaluated in healthy volunteers using placebo patches. Placebo transdermal nitroglycerin patches (Transderm-Nitro 5 placebo, Ciba Pharmaceutical Company; Nitro-Dur 10 cm2 placebo, Key Pharmaceuticals; and Nitrodisc 5 placebo, Searle Laboratories) were supplied by the manufacturers. Eighty-two healthy subjects were randomly assigned to begin using one of the three brands of patches. Using a Latin-square crossover design, subjects applied each brand of patch daily for five days and crossed over to the other brands on study days 6 and 11. At the end of each study phase, subjects completed a written questionnaire designed to evaluate their overall acceptance of each brand of patch. A total of 80 subjects completed all three phases of the study. According to forced rank preference, 84% of subjects preferred the Ciba patch to one of the other two brands. Subjects judged the Ciba patch to be the easiest of the three brands to use and reported significantly fewer side effects and skin irritation while using the Ciba patch; they also preferred the size of the Ciba patch and experienced significantly fewer problems with adherence of the Ciba patch. A significant percentage of subjects indicated that they would prefer a transdermal patch over tablets or ointment. Most subjects preferred the Ciba patch over the Key patch or Searle patch.

screening.rationale: Empirical randomized crossover study in healthy volunteers using placebo transdermal patches to study acceptance, side effects, and adherence—placebo/nocebo-related outcomes were the object of study.

classification.summary: Compared three brands of placebo transdermal nitroglycerin patches in a Latin-square crossover in healthy volunteers and found clear preferences and fewer reported side effects and adherence problems for one brand (Ciba).
classification.key_finding: 84% of subjects preferred the Ciba placebo patch and reported significantly fewer side effects, skin irritation, and adherence problems versus the other brands.

title: Oral carotenoid treatment in polymorphous light eruption: a cross-over comparison with oxychloroquine and placebo.
abstract: During 3 consecutive summers, patients from a total group of 40 persons with polymorphous light eruptions (PMLE) participated in a randomized, double-blind, cross-over study comparing the sun-protective effect of placebo capsules, a chloroquine derivative (200 mg daily of oxychloroquine), and a carotenoid preparation (betacarotene and canthaxanthine in a daily total dose of 100 mg). A total of 35 carotenoid, 38 chloroquine, and 27 placebo treatment periods were registered. Full freedom from sun sensitivity was obtained during 6 carotenoid and 8 chloroquine periods, but never with placebo treatment. In addition, a partial sun tolerance was induced in 17 carotenoid periods, 15 chloroquine periods, and in 14 placebo treatment periods.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind crossover trial that compared placebo capsules with active treatments and reported placebo-period responses, making placebo response an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial in 40 PMLE patients compared carotenoid, oxychloroquine, and placebo across summer periods and reported partial sun-tolerance during placebo periods but no full freedom from sensitivity with placebo.
classification.key_finding: Found partial sun tolerance in 14 of 27 placebo treatment periods, whereas full freedom occurred in 6 carotenoid and 8 chloroquine periods but in none with placebo.

title: Biofeedback: the ultimate placebo?
journal: The Australian nurses' journal. Royal Australian Nursing Federation

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the article's main topic is whether biofeedback functions as a placebo, qualifying as conceptual/commentary on placebo science despite missing abstract.

classification.summary: Discusses whether biofeedback operates via placebo mechanisms and considered implications for pain management and nursing practice.

title: Controlled comparison of short-wave diathermy treatment with osteopathic treatment in non-specific low back pain.
abstract: The effectiveness of spinal manipulation carried out by a non-medical qualified osteopath was compared with that of short-wave diathermy (SWD) and a placebo (detuned SWD) in 109 patients with low back pain. More than half the subjects in each of the 3 treatment groups benefited immediately from therapy. Significant improvements were observed in the 3 groups at the end of 2 weeks' treatment, and these were still apparent at 12 weeks. The outcome of treatment was unrelated to the initial severity or duration of pain or to the trend of pain towards deterioration or improvement. It is, therefore, unlikely that the results simply reflect the natural history of low back pain. Benefits obtained with osteopathy and SWD in this study may have been achieved through a placebo effect.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial included a detuned SWD placebo arm and reported improvements in the placebo group, discussing placebo as a likely mechanism, so placebo response/effect is an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared osteopathy, short-wave diathermy, and detuned (placebo) SWD in 109 low back pain patients and found all groups improved at 2 and 12 weeks, suggesting benefits may reflect placebo effects.
classification.key_finding: All three groups showed significant improvement at 2 and 12 weeks; placebo (detuned SWD) produced similar benefits to active treatments.

title: The placebo and the therapeutic uses of faith.
abstract: The holistic movement in modern medicine has raised questions concerning the very character of the religion-medicine dialogue. A truly mutual interaction between theology and medicine must require of the theologian a serious interest in and understanding of medicine if the notion of the body-mind unity is to be taken seriously from the point of view of pastoral care. This paper suggests that this discussion may be enriched by a theological analysis of the placebo, which has lately been the subject of controversy within medical circles. Finally, it is suggested that the value of the placebo reposes in its serving as a symbol of the dynamics of faith in medical care.

screening.rationale: The paper's main aim is a theological analysis of the placebo and its role in faith and medical care, making it a conceptual/theoretical piece about placebo science.

classification.summary: Argues that theological analysis of the placebo can enrich medicine and that the placebo functions as a symbol of faith and the dynamics of pastoral care.

title: The solid gold placebo.
journal: The New York state dental journal

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms explicitly reference placebos and TMJ/dental context, suggesting the paper's main subject concerns placebo use (likely a case report/review) despite missing abstract.

classification.summary: Reported on a clinical/case-level discussion of using a solid-gold placebo in dental/TMJ context, focusing on placebo use and implications.

title: Evaluating drug effectiveness in an office setting for children with attention deficit disorders.
abstract: Stimulant medications have been demonstrated to be useful in treating groups of children with attention deficit disorders, but placebo effects and situational differences in behavior in individual cases need to be followed and assessed. A simple procedure for systematically assessing these factors in the individual child in the office setting is described and illustrated. The procedure provides an objective means of determining the drug and placebo effects on the reported problem behavior and the differences between parent and teacher perceptions of the behavior.

screening.rationale: Paper described and illustrated a procedure to assess drug and placebo effects in individual children, making placebo effects an object of study rather than an incidental comparator.

classification.summary: Described a simple office-based procedure for systematically assessing drug and placebo effects and parent/teacher differences in individual children with ADHD.

title: Treatment of infantile colic with surface active substance (simethicone).
abstract: The effect of Simethicone on "colicky" (n = 27) infants was tested in a double-blind cross-over study. Three different parameters were used to measure the efficiency of the treatment: interviews, 24-hour records and behavioral observations. No effects of Simethicone on the symptoms of infantile colic could be demonstrated. However, 67% of the infants improved during the treatment, which could be ascribed to a high-grade placebo-effect.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial explicitly analyzed lack of drug effect and reported a large improvement during treatment attributed to a placebo effect/response in infants with colic, meeting inclusion criteria for placebo response/placebo science.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind crossover trial in 27 infants with colic and found no simethicone effect, though 67% improved during treatment which authors attributed to a strong placebo response.
classification.key_finding: No benefit of simethicone versus placebo; 67% of infants improved during treatment, interpreted as a high placebo response.

title: Requests for hypnotic drugs and placebo response in elderly hospital in-patients.
abstract: Requests for night sedation and the use of placebo as first line drug management were studied prospectively in 1174 consecutive elderly hospital in-patients. Of the 390 (33.2%) patients requesting sleeping pills in hospital, 37 were subsequently satisfied without the prescription of additional medication. A further 216 patients were entirely satisfied with a placebo capsule during all of their hospital stay. An 'active' hypnotic drug was required by only 137 patients, many of whom were noisy and disturbing other patients in the ward. Most of the active hypnotic drugs prescribed to elderly hospital patients are unnecessary and a majority of those requesting hypnotics consistently respond to placebo. There remains a need for greater education of patients, nurses and doctors in the non-pharmacological management of sleep disorders.

screening.rationale: Prospective empirical study that measured responses to placebo hypnotic capsules in elderly hospital in-patients, making placebo response the object of study.

classification.summary: Studied 1174 elderly hospital in-patients prospectively and found that many requesting sleeping pills were satisfied with placebo capsules without needing active hypnotics.
classification.key_finding: 216 of 1174 patients were entirely satisfied with a placebo capsule during their hospital stay, while only 137 required an active hypnotic.

title: In support of placebos: making do with make-believe.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH term indicate the article's main subject is placebo use in clinical practice (placebo science/ethics), meeting inclusion for placebo_science_other despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discussed and argued in favor of placebo use in clinical nursing practice, focusing on physician–patient relations and the role of placebo effects.

title: Nutritional supplementation with megadoses of vitamin B6. Effective therapy, placebo, or potentiator of neuropathy?

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available to determine whether placebo/nocebo was a primary aim or merely mentioned in a case report about pyridoxine and neuropathy.

classification.summary: Case report raised the question whether high-dose vitamin B6 effects on neuropathy were therapeutic, placebo-driven, or potentiating, but no abstract was available to confirm findings.

title: Medication and transitional phenomena.
abstract: Winnicott's concept of transitional phenomena is employed as a means of further understanding the effect of medicine and the medication-giving process itself. Particular facets examined include the "soothing" function of medication, the placebo effect, and medication compliance, as well as countertransference difficulties encountered in administering the medicine. Medication as a transitional object is viewed largely as a creation along the self-object interface, with the "potential space" between patient and therapist recapitulating aspects of the original dyad. This usage of medicine as a transitional object, or its ultimate abandonment as such, is presented in terms of the vicissitudes of internal object relations, with clinical case examples to clarify particular issues.

screening.rationale: Paper used Winnicottian theory and clinical case reports to analyze the placebo effect and medication-as-transitional-object, making placebo phenomena a primary subject rather than an incidental mention.

classification.summary: Applied Winnicott's transitional phenomena to conceptualize medication as a transitional object and discussed the placebo effect and medication compliance through clinical case examples.

title: Credibility of placebo transcutaneous nerve stimulation and acupuncture.
abstract: In a study comparing the credibility of acupuncture and sham transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) within a group of chronic pain patients, equal suggestion of the sham TNS was achieved by incorporating a visual display and strong verbal suggestion into the placebo treatment. The analgesic effect of placebo is a confounding factor in controlled trials of physical methods of pain relief, and the use of sham therapy distinguishable from active therapy requires that the placebo be validated as a true control for the non-specific components that constitute the placebo aspect of the active treatment. This study uses a questionnaire designed to assess patient expectancy of effectiveness and concludes that sham TNS with strong visual and verbal suggestion may be a valid placebo for controlled studies of the analgesic effect of acupuncture.

screening.rationale: Empirical study directly investigated placebo credibility/expectancy of sham TNS versus acupuncture in chronic pain patients, addressing placebo control validation (placebo science).

classification.summary: Compared credibility and expectancy for sham TNS versus acupuncture in chronic pain patients using a questionnaire and found sham TNS with visual display and strong verbal suggestion produced comparable expectancy to acupuncture.
classification.key_finding: Found that sham TNS with enhanced visual and verbal suggestion yielded similar patient expectancy of effectiveness to acupuncture, supporting its validity as a control.

title: Truth telling, placebos, and deception: ethical and legal issues in practice.
abstract: The issue of truth-telling is very complex. There is variance among patients in the amount of information they want to be told and variance among professionals in the amount of information they want to tell. Truth is conditioned by our knowledge limits and understanding. Technological advances in health care have made this arena even more complex. Placebos have been viewed traditionally as a kind of benign deception. Few studies have looked at treatments and tests as placebos. There are many myths associated with placebos and placebo therapy. There are five primary theories for withholding the truth or promoting deception with patients. Ethical and legal principles generally support veracity and the concept of a duty to tell the truth. One of the remaining issues is whether the placebo effect can be achieved without deception.

screening.rationale: Narrative/theoretical article addressing ethics, deception, and whether placebo effects can be achieved without deception, so it meets the 'placebo science' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical and legal issues of truth-telling, deception, and placebo use in clinical practice and queried whether placebo effects could be achieved without deception.

title: A comparison of behavioral, meditation, and placebo control relaxation training procedures.

screening.rationale: Title indicates comparison including a 'placebo control' relaxation procedure but no abstract or full text available to confirm whether placebo/placebo response was a primary object of study versus merely a control.

classification.summary: Title compared behavioral, meditation, and placebo control relaxation training procedures but no abstract was available to confirm aims or findings.

title: The analgesic effects of aspirin and placebo on experimentally induced tooth pulp pain.
abstract: We examined the relative analgesic potency of aspirin and placebo in a within-subject-repeated-measure experiment using a precision tooth pulp stimulation technique with long-term stability (r = 0.93) for more than two months between measures. The attenuation of pain perception was evaluated using a standardized magnitude estimation procedure and constructing an individual psychophysical function for each trial. The data were fit equally well by either a straight line (Y = mX + b) or a power function (Y = mXa + b). Using the line fit and distribution insensitive conservative statistical tests, the effect of each treatment was compared to baseline and the treatments were compared to each other. In randomized, double-blind trials we found reliable effects of both aspirin (p less than 0.001) and placebo (p less than 0.001) but no difference (p = 0.08) between these two treatments. However, on an individual basis, 12 of 17 subjects displayed a larger analgesic response to aspirin than to placebo (p less than 0.05).

screening.rationale: Within-subject randomized double-blind experiment directly measured placebo (placebo arm pre-post) analgesic responses and compared them to aspirin.

classification.summary: Conducted randomized, double-blind within-subject tests of aspirin and placebo on experimental tooth-pulp pain and found reliable analgesia from both, with no overall difference between treatments.
classification.key_finding: Both aspirin and placebo produced significant analgesia versus baseline (p<0.001 each); group comparison showed no reliable difference (p=0.08), though 12/17 individuals had larger responses to aspirin (p<0.05).

title: Attrition and its consequences in a clinical trial of placebo, imipramine, and phenelzine.

screening.rationale: Insufficient information (no abstract) to determine whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or merely reported attrition in an RCT where placebo served only as a control.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported on attrition and its consequences in a randomized trial comparing placebo, imipramine, and phenelzine for depressive disorder.

title: Chronomodulatory infradian synchronization by placebo or ACTH 1-17 of Musca autumnalis mortality on shifted lighting regimens.
abstract: The face fly, Musca autumnalis, exposed to shifts of an LD16:8 lighting schedule at varying intervals, whether previously untreated or given placebo or ACTH 1-17 treatment, before the initiation of shifts, exhibits an infradian frequency response in mortality. At overall 50% mortality, a periodicity of approximately 4.5 days is found for flies exposed to placebo or ACTH 1-17 as a response to the shift interval. As compared to controls, the mortality of flies treated with placebo or ACTH 1-17 is delayed. Not all shift schedules are detrimental; some are actually beneficial.

screening.rationale: Empirical nonhuman-animal experiment that compared placebo (vs control and ACTH) and reported causal effects of placebo treatment on mortality periodicity under shifted lighting, so placebo is an object of study.

classification.summary: Reported that face flies given placebo or ACTH 1-17 before shifted LD16:8 lighting showed an infradian (~4.5 day) mortality periodicity and delayed mortality compared with controls.
classification.key_finding: Placebo-treated flies exhibited delayed mortality and a ~4.5-day infradian periodicity in mortality under shifted lighting.

title: The use of placebos in randomized clinical trials.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the paper's primary focus is ethical and methodological issues about use of placebos in RCTs, meeting the 'placebo science' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical and methodological issues surrounding the use of placebos in randomized clinical trials, including deception and informed consent.

title: Medicine's humble humbug: four periods in the understanding of the placebo.

screening.rationale: Title and publication type indicate a historical analysis of placebo concepts, so the paper's main subject is the placebo and meets the 'placebo science' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Reviews four historical periods in the understanding of the placebo and its role in medicine.

title: Control theory and multiple placebo effects.
journal: International journal of psychiatry in medicine
abstract: The importance of the placebo in medicine is well documented, yet our understanding of placebo effects remains limited. One obstacle to a greater understanding is the fact that the phrase "placebo effect" has been used to refer to a number of qualitatively distinct behavioral events. Thus, different theories have been promulgated, each one tending to explain a selective portion of the placebo phenomenon. To help clarify matters, three kinds of placebo effects are described, and theories that have been used to explain them are reviewed. Limitations of these theories are then discussed, and a general model of placebo effects, based on a control theory perspective, is presented. Some implications and limitations of this model are outlined.

screening.rationale: The paper is a theoretical/modeling article whose primary aim is to explain placebo effects via a control-theory model, so it meets the 'placebo science more broadly' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Proposes a control-theory model that integrates conditioning, attention, and expectancy accounts to clarify multiple placebo effects and critiques existing theories.

title: The antagonistic placebo response to alcohol cues.
abstract: The classical conditioning model of drug tolerance makes a strong prediction of an antagonistic placebo response, or a placebo response that is opposite in direction to the effect of alcohol. In an initial experiment, 85 normal social drinkers consumed near beer (0% alcohol) while autonomic measures were recorded continuously. Subjects who reported mild intoxication (n = 11) showed a significant decrease in heart rate from predrinking baseline compared to subjects who did not report intoxication (n = 57). In a replication study with a suitable control group, subjects who received near beer and reported mild intoxication (n = 8) showed a significant heart rate and electrodermal response opposite in direction to the autonomic effects of alcohol compared to a control group that received a soft drink (n = 10). The antagonist placebo response challenges current conceptualizations of placebo responding, and has implications for classical conditioning theories of alcoholism.

screening.rationale: Empirical human experiments explicitly tested placebo/antagonistic placebo responses to nonalcoholic 'near beer' with autonomic and subjective outcomes, addressing placebo mechanisms (classical conditioning).

classification.summary: Reported that presentation of nonalcoholic 'near beer' produced an antagonistic placebo response: participants who felt mildly intoxicated showed heart-rate decreases and electrodermal changes opposite to alcohol's effects, replicated with a soft-drink control.
classification.key_finding: Found decreased heart rate and altered electrodermal response in 'near beer' recipients reporting mild intoxication, an antagonistic placebo effect consistent with classical conditioning.

title: Conditioned placebo responses.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: Following earlier animal research, we attempt to condition placebo effects in human subjects. Four groups of 8 voluntary subjects were told that the experimenters would test a powerful new analgesic cream over three sessions by assessing its ability to reduce experimentally induced pain. The analgesic cream was, in fact, a placebo. In the first session all subjects were tested with and without the cream to assess their placebo response. In the second session, to condition two groups (with differing stimulation levels) to experience pain relief in response to the placebo, we repeatedly paired a reduction in nocioceptive stimulation with placebo administration. (Subjects were unaware that stimulation levels were manipulated). To condition the other two groups (with different stimulation levels) to experience an exacerbation of the pain, we paired an increase in nocioceptive stimulation with placebo administration. In the third session, all subjects were again tested for placebo response. Results suggested that placebo responses are conditionable in the laboratory in both a positive and negative direction. The clinical implications of a learning theory of placebo behavior are discussed.

screening.rationale: Empirical human experiment whose primary aim was to condition placebo (and nocebo) responses using paired changes in nociceptive stimulation and a topical placebo.

classification.summary: Conditioned placebo analgesia and conditioned increases in pain were induced in healthy volunteers by pairing reductions or increases in nociceptive stimulation with an inert topical cream, producing bidirectional placebo/nocebo responses.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo responses could be learned by classical conditioning, yielding both analgesia and pain exacerbation in different groups (N=32).

title: Alcohol and aggression in a group interaction.
abstract: Forty-four volunteer male subjects participated in groups of four along with two experimental confederates in a group interaction after consuming either 1.32 mg/kg of 95% USP alcohol or placebo. According to a balanced-placebo design, subjects were told they were either consuming alcohol or placebo. The task of one confederate was to initiate conversation and distract subjects from monitoring their state of intoxication while the second confederate's role was to antagonize subjects at a prescribed time. Sessions were videotaped and rated for frequency of positive and negative interactions and subjects completed rating scales evaluating each other. The results failed to show an expectancy effect on any measures; however, there was an alcohol effect seen in an increase in negative interactions as well as positive interactions and a significant expectancy X alcohol interaction for negative ratings of the provocative confederate. In those groups where the manipulation matched the expectation, alcohol-told alcohol and placebo-told placebo the confederate was seen more negatively than in the mixed groups. An attributional explanation for the results is offered and the generality of the alcohol-expectancy phenomenon questioned.

screening.rationale: Used a balanced-placebo design manipulating intoxication and told expectancy to test expectancy/placebo mechanisms (active-drug context manipulation), so placebo/expectancy was a primary object of study.

classification.summary: Conducted a balanced-placebo group interaction study (N=44 men) manipulating alcohol administration and told expectancy; alcohol increased both negative and positive interactions, while expectancy had no main effect though it interacted with alcohol for negative confederate ratings.
classification.key_finding: Alcohol increased observed interaction negativity and positivity; expectancy showed no main effect but interacted with alcohol on negative ratings when expectation matched actual beverage.

title: Placebo therapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis.
abstract: Eighteen postmenopausal osteoporotic (PMO) women on placebo therapy were followed for 1 year. Serial measurements of calcium balance and kinetics, bone histomorphometry, photon absorptiometry, and radiogrammetry were obtained. Few significant changes in balance and kinetics or bone histology were seen in these women over time. Photon absorptiometry and radiogrammetry of the femoral cortex showed a significant annual bone loss however. When compared with premenopausal and healthy postmenopausal women, the annual bone loss in those with PMO was significantly greater. The ability of balance studies, photon absorptiometry, and radiogrammetry to predict the magnitude of this bone loss was similar. Finally, there was an illustration of the use of the estimated variance provided by this study for estimating sample size for future studies.

screening.rationale: Single-group longitudinal study of placebo-treated postmenopausal osteoporotic women reporting placebo-arm changes and variance, meeting inclusion for placebo_response.

classification.summary: Followed 18 postmenopausal osteoporotic women on placebo for one year and measured bone balance, histomorphometry and imaging, finding significant femoral cortical bone loss but few other changes.
classification.key_finding: Found significant annual femoral cortex bone loss on photon absorptiometry and radiogrammetry despite otherwise minimal changes in bone histology and balance.

title: The effects of naloxone on opiate and placebo analgesia in healthy volunteers.
abstract: Two double blind cross-over studies were performed using a submaximal effort tourniquet test (SETT) in healthy volunteers to investigate the role of endogenous opioids in placebo analgesia. In the first study IV naloxone significantly inhibited analgesia, miosis and sedation produced by the opioid dipipanone 10 mg in 12 subjects. In the second naloxone, which did not produce hyperalgesia, failed to inhibit significant placebo analgesia in 12 subjects. The results do not support the involvement of endogenous opioids in ischemic limb pain or placebo analgesia under these conditions.

screening.rationale: Primary double-blind crossover experiment directly tested placebo analgesia and whether naloxone (pharmacological manipulation) blocks it, addressing mechanisms of placebo analgesia.

classification.summary: Conducted two double-blind crossover SETT studies in healthy volunteers and found naloxone blocked opioid analgesia but did not block significant placebo analgesia, arguing against endogenous opioid mediation under these conditions.
classification.key_finding: Naloxone inhibited dipipanone analgesia but failed to block placebo-induced analgesia in healthy volunteers (placebo analgesia remained significant).

title: Overestimations of hypnotic drug effects by insomniacs--a hypothesis.
abstract: Data on subjective estimates and polygraphic measures of total sleep time and sleep latency were collected from the literature and analyzed for accordance or discrepancy between subjective and objective (EEG-based) mean values in experiments on acute treatment of insomnia by benzodiazepine hypnotics. In baseline placebo conditions there was a tendency to overestimate the disturbance of sleep. After drug administration, sleeping was overestimated. Within both subjective and objective measures, the magnitude of drug effects was correlated with poor initial sleep. If discrepancies between subjective and objective measures per se were analyzed, a number of correlational factors led to the hypothesis that psychological characteristics of a given population play a primary role: populations overestimating their sleep disturbances also tended to overestimate hypnotic drug effects. However, overestimations of drug effects were not correlated with type of drug or objective measures of sleep disturbance before treatment.

screening.rationale: Secondary analysis of published sleep trials focused on subjective vs objective (placebo-baseline included) estimates and hypothesized psychological biases in placebo/baseline overestimation, meeting placebo-science criteria.

classification.summary: Analyzed published data on subjective and EEG sleep measures in benzodiazepine insomnia studies and hypothesized that psychological characteristics lead insomniacs to overestimate both sleep disturbance at baseline and hypnotic drug effects.
classification.key_finding: Found that insomniac samples tended to overestimate sleep disturbance in baseline/placebo conditions and to overestimate hypnotic drug effects subjectively, with magnitude correlated with poor initial sleep.
